note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Gradual reduction in hearing in the left ear for ~6 weeks.
  - Intermittent left-sided tinnitus; patient reports “some things trigger it,” citing watching TV/listening to music; later states those activities “solve” the ringing (conflict noted).
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Symptoms on and off over 6 weeks.
  - Prior similar episode approximately 1 year ago lasting a couple of days; resolved spontaneously (details unclear).
- ENT symptoms:
  - Hearing: Reduced on the left; right ear perceived as normal.
  - Tinnitus: Left-sided, intermittent; unclear relationship to sound exposure (trigger vs relief—conflict noted).
  - Dizziness/imbalance: Mild, intermittent “off balance”; denies true room-spinning vertigo. Initially mentioned feeling “a bit sick,” later states not nausea-type dizziness (conflict noted).
  - Ear pain: Denies.
  - Ear discharge: Denies.
  - Fever: Denies.
  - No documentation of ear itching, throat symptoms, nasal/ocular symptoms, dyspnea/stridor, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling, ear fullness/pressure, or neck pain/swelling.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - Brief similar episode ~1 year ago; no documented treatment; resolved.
  - No prior ED visits/hospitalizations or injection therapies noted.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: Not documented.
  - Medications: Not documented.
  - Denies using cotton buds/Q-tips for ear cleaning.
- Any relevant social context:
  - Telehealth visit; patient in a private location. No mention of accompaniment.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: Not reported.
- Airway/breathing: No distress reported; no stridor/noisy breathing mentioned.
- Mental status/associated features: No syncope reported; dizziness as above.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded (telehealth; no otoscopy performed).
- Presence of another person: Not stated.

Assessment:
- Unilateral left-sided hearing reduction with intermittent unilateral tinnitus and mild intermittent imbalance over 6 weeks.
- Differential considerations discussed by clinician include cerumen impaction vs pathology within the ear/balance system; requires otoscopic examination to rule out obstructive causes.
- Justification: 6-week unilateral symptoms; denies pain/discharge/fever; intermittent tinnitus; mild non-vertiginous imbalance; prior brief episode ~1 year ago.
- Conflicts noted: 
  - Tinnitus relationship to audiovisual stimuli—reported as both a trigger and a relief.
  - Nausea—initially “a bit sick” vs later denying nausea-type dizziness.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Arrange face-to-face clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopic examination to assess for cerumen impaction or other external/middle ear pathology.
  - Clinician to place a tinnitus information leaflet link in the visit notes; patient asked to review prior to visit.
- Specific instructions provided:
  - Patient to call the support team (number to be placed in notes) to schedule the in-person appointment.
  - If any problems arise before the clinic visit, book another video appointment.
- Escalation criteria/red flags:
  - Not specifically discussed/documented.
- Follow-up:
  - In-person evaluation by another GP/clinician within 4–5 days with review of current notes and focus on ear examination.
  - Further management to be guided by otoscopic findings and discussion of tinnitus information reviewed by patient.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Full allergy list; current medication list (including ototoxic agents); past medical/ENT and surgical history.
  - Detailed otologic history: ear fullness/pressure, hyperacusis, pulsatile vs non-pulsatile tinnitus, noise/occupational exposure, recent infections, barotrauma, head trauma, family history of hearing loss.
  - Objective findings: otoscopy, tuning fork tests, audiometry, vestibular/neurologic exam, vitals.
  - Clear documentation of nausea vs no nausea; clarification of tinnitus triggers vs relief.
- Internal conflicts:
  - Tinnitus reportedly “triggered” by TV/music vs later “solved” by TV/music.
  - Nausea initially implied (“a bit sick”) vs later denied (“not the kind of dizziness you get with nausea”).
- Transcript quality:
  - Some responses were unclear or incomplete; minor ambiguities and possible transcription errors (e.g., “solve” vs “set off”).
